endorsements.quote: We advocate for hospitals to establish formal oversight mechanisms, such as dedicated AI committees, to ensure the safe implementation of AI systems.

To better align AI development with clinical ethics, we propose the incorporation of multidisciplinary boards comprising clinicians, patients, ethicists, and technological experts, who should be responsible for systematically reviewing algorithmic behaviour in critical care, assessing the risks of bias, and promoting transparency in decision-making processes.
The third important aspect is liability, identifying who should be held accountable if an AI decision or a human decision based on AI leads to harm.
The first step toward integration is to understand how clinicians interact with AI and to design systems that complement, rather than disrupt, clinical reasoning [ 32 ].

To accelerate AI adoption and trust, we advocate that physicians must be trained to interpret outputs under uncertainty—using frameworks like plausibility, consistency with known biology, and alignment with consolidated clinical reasoning—rather than expecting full explainability [ 49 ].
In addition to undergraduate education, it is essential to train experienced physicians, nurses, and other allied health professional [ 43 ].

A straightforward example of the latter is the development of interpretable, real-time dashboards that synthetize complex multidimensional data into visual formats, thereby enhancing clinicians’ situational awareness without overwhelming them.

unlisted_practices: Include data science and AI fundamental concepts, methods, and limitations in the core medical degree curriculum.
Hold AI research to the same methodological standards as other areas of medical research, with greater accountability from peer reviewers and journals.
Adopt reporting and validation frameworks such as TRIPOD-AI, PROBAST-AI, CONSORT-AI, and STARD-AI and disseminate them through critical care societies and courses.
Adopt higher methodological standards for critical care AI research, including pre-registered AI trials, prospective validation in diverse ICU populations, and standardized performance benchmarks.
Retain data ownership within healthcare institutions and recognize patients and providers as stakeholders in the value their data creates.
Adopt recognized data interoperability standards such as OMOP CDM and FHIR across hospitals, device makers, and EHR vendors.
Prioritize data safety, security, and privacy in AI deployment.
Support open-source AI models with funding, academic recognition, and regulatory support to reduce dependence on proprietary algorithms.
Build collaborative multi-ICU data networks, federated learning, and shared datasets at national and international level.
Establish partnerships among healthcare institutions, technology companies, and governments to support AI development and deployment.
Professional societies and regulators should establish specific clinical practice guidelines for AI in critical care covering model validation, clinician-AI collaboration, and accountability.
Regulation should be adaptive and proportionate, focused on risk-based oversight and continuous post-deployment monitoring.
Require mandatory reporting of AI performance and create hospital-based AI safety committees.

Require AI vendors to provide post-marketing surveillance plans and report serious incidents within a predefined time window, with standardized monitoring protocols, embedded incident reporting tools, performance registries, and regular audits.
Adopt continuous risk assessment and real-time auditing of dynamic AI models internationally.
Require a rigorous regulatory evaluation of safety and efficacy before clinical use of AI products, and mandatory continuous post-market evaluation.
Regulators should provide clear rules on liability and insurance for AI-related harm.
Involve patients and societal representatives in defining the goals and limits of AI in healthcare through a social contract.
Address the AI divide through supranational coordination, grants, training networks, and equitable allocation of AI resources.
Develop AI to reduce administrative burden and increase time for patient-physician communication.
Start ICU AI integration with human-AI augmentation, in which AI supports rather than replaces clinicians.
Intensivists should lead the development of frameworks to measure fairness, assess bias, and set acceptable thresholds for AI uncertainty.

screen.reason: Expert consensus statement providing actionable recommendations and a framework for implementing AI ethically and effectively in critical care medicine.
